title: Bindings, Not Boxes
goal: How Rust names values: immutable by default, mut to change, shadowing to rebind.

sections.text: You already know variables. Rust calls them bindings, and the difference matters: `let x = 5;` binds a name to a value, and by default that binding cannot change. Reassigning it is a compile error, not a style complaint.

sections.code:
let x = 5;
x = 6;              // error E0384: cannot assign twice
sections.caption: Immutable is the default.

sections.text: When a value genuinely needs to change, say so: `let mut x = 5;` allows `x = 6;` later. The `mut` is documentation the compiler enforces. Reading unfamiliar code, every mutation site is announced at the binding.

The third tool is shadowing: a second `let` with the same name creates a new binding and the old one disappears. Shadowing may change the type, which mutation never can. Turning `"3"` into `3` while keeping the name is normal Rust.

sections.code:
let number = "three";
let number = 3;      // new binding, new type - fine
sections.caption: Shadowing rebinds the name.

sections.text: For fixed values there is `const`: it needs an explicit type, uses SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE, and can live outside any function. You will use all three forms in the next puzzles.

explanation: How Rust names values: immutable by default, mut to change, shadowing to rebind.
